cards.front: A {{c1::unicellular}} organism is made of one cell, and a multicellular organism is made of many.
cards.back: Bacteria, many algae and many protists are unicellular.
cards.quote: A unicellular organism is made of one cell, and a multicellular organism is made of many.
cards.section: Explain: one cell that does it all

cards.front: How can a unicellular organism such as a Paramecium carry out every life process with only one cell?
cards.back: It uses different structures within that one cell for different jobs.
cards.why: Cilia, food vacuoles and a contractile vacuole are examples of such structures.
cards.quote: A unicellular organism carries out every life process inside one cell, using different structures within that cell for different jobs.
cards.section: Explain: one cell that does it all

cards.front: How does a Paramecium take in food?
cards.back: Cilia beat together like oars and sweep food such as bacteria into a groove. The food is digested in food vacuoles.
cards.quote: Food such as bacteria is swept into a groove and digested in food vacuoles.
cards.section: Explain: one cell that does it all

cards.front: Why does water keep moving into a Paramecium living in pond water?
cards.back: Pond water has fewer dissolved particles than the cell, so water moves in by osmosis.
cards.quote: Pond water has fewer dissolved particles than the cell, so water keeps moving in by osmosis
cards.section: Explain: one cell that does it all

cards.front: What does a contractile vacuole do in a Paramecium?
cards.back: It is a sac that fills with the extra water that enters the cell and squeezes it out.
cards.quote: A contractile vacuole is a sac that fills with this extra water and squeezes it out.
cards.section: Explain: one cell that does it all

cards.front: {{c1::Binary fission}} is reproducing without a partner: one cell divides into two.
cards.quote: Binary fission is reproducing without a partner: one cell divides into two.
cards.section: Explain: one cell that does it all

cards.front: In a model where each cell in a group has just one job, every cell that takes in food is removed. Can the remaining cells keep the group growing?
cards.back: No, in the model. Sharing work creates dependence.
cards.why: If no cell does one required job, the other specialists do not replace it.
cards.quote: Sharing work creates dependence: if no cell does one required job, the other specialists do not replace it.
cards.section: Explore: share out life’s jobs

cards.front: A {{c1::tissue}} is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is several tissues working together.
cards.quote: a tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is several tissues working together
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: What is an organ system, and where does it sit in the levels of organization?
cards.back: A set of related organs. Order: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
cards.quote: an organ system is a set of related organs.
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: A layer of similar cells covers a plant root, and root hair cells grow from it. Which level of organization is the layer, and which is the whole root?
cards.back: The layer is a tissue. The whole root is an organ.
cards.why: An organ is built from several tissues.
cards.quote: The layer of similar cells is a tissue. The whole root is an organ, built from several tissues.
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: A muscle cell is specialized for shortening. Does it still take in food and make ATP?
cards.back: Yes. Specialized means especially fitted for a job, not limited to only one job.
cards.quote: specialized means especially fitted for a job, not limited to only one job.
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: How does the long, thin axon of a neuron fit its job?
cards.back: It carries signals long distances, such as from the spine to the foot.
cards.quote: Carries signals long distances, such as from the spine to the foot
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: How does the shape of a mature red blood cell fit its job?
cards.back: A small, flexible, dented disc gives a large surface for oxygen to cross and bends to squeeze through narrow vessels.
cards.quote: Large surface for oxygen to cross; bends to squeeze through narrow vessels
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: How does the structure of a skeletal muscle cell fit its job?
cards.back: A very long cylinder with many nuclei, packed with protein fibres that shorten together to pull on bone.
cards.quote: Packed with protein fibres that shorten together to pull on bone
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: How does a root hair cell's long tube shape help the plant?
cards.back: It adds surface touching the soil, where water and minerals enter.
cards.quote: Adds surface touching the soil, where water and minerals enter
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: Guard cells curve around a pore in a leaf. If they change shape, what can they control?
cards.back: They open or close the pore, controlling gas movement through the leaf surface.
cards.quote: They can open or close the pore, controlling gas movement through the leaf surface.
cards.section: Explain: specialized cells, from tissues to systems

cards.front: A skin cell and a nerve cell come from the same person. What is true about their DNA, and what makes them different?
cards.back: Nearly all body cells with a nucleus carry essentially the same DNA. They differ because each kind uses a different set of genes.
cards.quote: Nearly all body cells with a nucleus carry essentially the same DNA, but each kind of cell uses a different set of genes
cards.section: Explain: same DNA, different genes

cards.front: In cells with the same DNA, what is gene expression, and what happens to many genes in each cell?
cards.back: Gene expression is the use of a gene's instructions to make a product such as a protein. Many genes stay unused in each cell.
cards.quote: Many genes stay unused in each cell.
cards.section: Explain: same DNA, different genes

cards.front: A student notes that mature human red blood cells have no nucleus and says every body cell must have different DNA. Is that right?
cards.back: No. The mature red blood cell is an exception, but most body cells with a nucleus share essentially the same DNA.
cards.why: A maturing red blood cell pushes out its nucleus, and mitochondria, so no DNA is left.
cards.quote: A maturing red blood cell pushes out its nucleus and also gets rid of its mitochondria
cards.section: Exceptions to the shared-DNA model

cards.front: A human oocyte has a mean diameter of 115 micrometres. A red blood cell is about 7.5 micrometres across. About how many times wider is the oocyte?
cards.back: 115 ÷ 7.5 is about 15, so about 15 times wider.
cards.why: Dividing gives how many times wider; subtracting only gives a difference in micrometres.
cards.quote: For the egg, 115 ÷ 7.5 is about 15.
cards.section: Elaborate: measuring specialized cells

cards.front: An Arabidopsis root hair on a young seedling averages 0.49 mm long and 9.9 µm wide. About how many times longer than wide is it?
cards.back: 0.49 mm = 490 µm. Then 490 ÷ 9.9 is about 50, so about 50 times longer than wide.
cards.why: Convert units first. This compares pooled means, not one hair.
cards.quote: Convert the units first: 0.49 millimetres is 490 micrometres.
cards.section: Elaborate: measuring specialized cells

cards.front: A study gives mean human sperm head length (4.96 µm) and mean tail length (38.22 µm), each measured on its own. Can you add them to get the whole cell's mean length?
cards.back: No. Head plus tail leaves out the midpiece, which was measured separately.
cards.quote: The study measured the parts separately, so head plus tail leaves out the midpiece.
cards.section: Elaborate: measuring specialized cells

cards.front: Why should you be careful when comparing the rows of a table of published cell measurements?
cards.back: The rows come from different studies with different methods, not one survey.
cards.quote: The rows come from different studies with different methods, not one survey.
cards.section: Elaborate: measuring specialized cells

cards.front: How does Volvox carteri show division of labor with only two kinds of cells?
cards.back: About 1,000 to 2,000 small cells swim and make food but cannot divide. Up to 16 large cells are set aside for reproduction.
cards.quote: about 1,000 to 2,000 small cells swim and make food but can no longer divide, while up to 16 large cells are set aside for reproduction
cards.section: A bridge between one cell and many specialists

cards.front: About how many cells does a 70-kilogram reference adult man hold, according to two careful estimates?
cards.back: About 30 to 36 trillion cells.
cards.quote: A 70-kilogram reference adult man holds about 30 to 36 trillion cells
cards.section: How many cells and cell types?

cards.front: Textbooks often say there are about 200 kinds of cells, but a 2022 atlas counted more than 400. Why do the counts differ?
cards.back: The true number depends on how finely you sort the cells.
cards.why: The atlas sorted cells by the genes they use.
cards.quote: so the true number depends on how finely you sort.
cards.section: How many cells and cell types?

cards.front: Plan a fair test of whether radish seedlings on drier paper towels grow longer root hairs than seedlings on wetter towels. Name the variables, constants and control.
cards.back: Independent: how wet the towel is (for example 5 mL versus 15 mL of water). Dependent: root hair length, measured on the same part of each root with a scale in view. Constants: seed batch, seeds per dish, temperature, light, towel type, day measured. Control: dishes with the usual amount of water for sprouting seeds.
cards.why: Use several dishes per group, ten or more seedlings per dish, and a partner who codes the dishes.
cards.quote: Independent variable: how wet the paper towel is.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Immune cells cut and rejoin pieces of their DNA as they mature. Does this break the rule that nearly all body cells with a nucleus share essentially the same DNA?
cards.back: No. The rule says nearly all, and the lesson lists this as an exception, along with mature red blood cells that have no DNA left.
cards.why: Egg and sperm also carry one set of chromosomes, while most body cells carry two.
cards.quote: Some immune cells cut and rejoin pieces of their DNA as they mature
cards.section: Exceptions to the shared-DNA model

cards.front: Compare how a Paramecium and a muscle cell in your body each get all life's jobs done.
cards.back: The Paramecium holds every structure it needs in one cell. The muscle cell is specialized for shortening but still feeds and maintains itself, and relies on other specialized cells for other jobs.
cards.why: Specialized means fitted for a job, and shared work creates dependence.
cards.quote: A Paramecium survives alone because its one cell holds every structure it needs.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking
